report:
**Conclusion:** Your view is substantially justified if the claim implies a reliable or meaningful reduction in *abdominal/visceral* fat. Evidence does not convincingly show that CLA supplements produce clinically important belly-fat loss.

Early trials and an older meta-analysis found small average reductions in *total fat mass*, but human results were inconsistent—not the strong effects seen in animals. The meta-analysis did not establish a specific, dependable effect on abdominal fat:  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17490954/?uid=094f749f55f2d8s16

More importantly, a 2023 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis concluded that higher-quality studies did **not** demonstrate body-fat-lowering effects, and that any estimated weight/fat changes were small and may not be clinically important:  
https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366/S0007114523001861a.pdf/div-class-title-the-effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-dose-response-meta-analysis-div.pdf

The key distinction is that “body fat” outcomes are not necessarily abdominal or visceral fat. Studies use differing CLA isomer mixtures, doses, durations, populations, and measurement methods; direct abdominal-fat evidence is comparatively limited. Thus, a marketing claim that CLA *reduces abdominal fat* overstates the evidence.

NIH’s Office of Dietary Supplements includes CLA among weight-loss ingredients but emphasizes that supplement claims often exceed evidence and that established weight-loss approaches remain diet and physical activity:  
https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/WeightLoss-HealthProfessional/

So: CLA may have, at most, a small and uncertain effect on overall fat mass; it is not well supported as an effective abdominal-fat-reduction supplement.
